name: Reverse Armbar
description: Master the Reverse Armbar from North-South in BJJ. Step-by-step execution for this unique arm attack. Success rates: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
overview:
The Reverse Armbar from North-South represents a unique submission opportunity that exploits the perpendicular body alignment characteristic of this dominant pin position. Unlike the traditional armbar where you position your hips beside the opponent's head, the Reverse Armbar attacks the arm while your body remains aligned north-south, creating a breaking angle across your hips or chest that the opponent cannot easily defend.

This technique capitalizes on the arm control opportunities inherent to North-South position. When your opponent attempts to frame against your chest or push your hips away, they expose their arms to isolation and attack. The Reverse Armbar specifically targets arms that extend toward your hips or get caught in unfavorable positions during escape attempts. The attack vector differs from standard armbars, making it difficult for opponents who train primarily against conventional arm attacks.

Strategically, the Reverse Armbar serves as a complement to the North-South choke and kimura attacks. When opponents defend their neck by tucking their chin and framing with their arms, they become vulnerable to arm isolation. The technique works particularly well against opponents who create frames with their forearms, as these frames can be captured and converted into submission attempts. Understanding when to transition between these attacks creates a dangerous offensive network from North-South.
key_principles: Isolate the target arm before committing to the submission attempt
Create the breaking angle by positioning the arm across your hips or chest
Maintain heavy chest pressure throughout the attack to prevent escape
Control the opponent's wrist and elbow simultaneously for clean leverage
Use your body weight rather than arm strength to apply breaking pressure
Keep hips low and base wide to prevent bridging counters during the attack
Recognize the arm exposure windows during opponent's escape attempts
setup_requirements: Established North-South top control with chest pressure across opponent's upper body
Target arm isolated and extended toward your hip or trapped during frame attempt
Secure grip on opponent's wrist controlling their hand and preventing rotation
Control of opponent's elbow or upper arm preventing retraction
Base established to prevent bridge and roll counters during submission attempt
Opponent's opposite arm controlled or pinned to prevent defensive assistance

execution_steps.description: From North-South top, identify which arm has extended toward your hips or become exposed during their escape attempt - this becomes your target for the reverse armbar attack
execution_steps.timing: During opponent's frame or escape attempt

execution_steps.description: Grip the opponent's wrist firmly with your hand closest to their hips, ensuring their palm faces upward or inward to prevent them from rotating their elbow and escaping the attack angle
Use your other hand or your hip to trap their elbow in position against your body, preventing them from bending their arm or retracting it back toward their torso for defense

Position their arm so their elbow joint crosses your hips or lower chest, with their forearm pointing toward your head and their upper arm extending toward their body - this creates hyperextension leverage
Clamp your elbows tight to your body while maintaining wrist control, creating a unified structure where your entire torso controls their arm rather than relying solely on grip strength
Drive your hips upward while keeping their wrist pinned and elbow trapped, hyperextending their elbow joint by using your body as the fulcrum point - control the submission speed for training safety
If they tap, release immediately; if they begin escaping before you can finish, transition immediately to side control or continue to kimura control rather than losing position entirely

common_counters.counter: Opponent pulls elbow tight to body before you can isolate the arm
common_counters.your_response: Transition to kimura attack on the same arm or switch to North-South choke - their elbow defense often exposes their neck

common_counters.counter: Opponent bridges and rolls as you commit to the arm attack
common_counters.your_response: Maintain tight grip and ride the roll, potentially finishing the armbar from the resulting scramble or transitioning to mount

common_counters.counter: Opponent rotates their arm to align elbow with your attack angle, preventing hyperextension
common_counters.your_response: Adjust your hip position to find a new breaking angle, or switch grip to establish kimura control on the rotated arm

common_counters.counter: Opponent frames with opposite arm to create space and recover guard
common_counters.your_response: Pin the framing arm with your free hand while maintaining the reverse armbar grip, or release and reestablish heavy North-South pressure

common_errors.error: Releasing chest pressure to reach for the arm
common_errors.consequence: Opponent creates space and escapes to guard or turtle before you can secure the submission grip
common_errors.correction: Maintain heavy North-South pressure throughout - only attack arms that are already exposed without sacrificing position

common_errors.error: Attacking the arm with only grip strength instead of body position
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can power out of the submission or creates extended grip fighting that exhausts you
common_errors.correction: Position their arm across your hips or chest so your body weight creates the submission pressure, not just your hands

common_errors.error: Failing to control the wrist palm position
common_errors.consequence: Opponent rotates their arm to align with your force, eliminating the hyperextension angle and escaping the lock
common_errors.correction: Ensure palm faces upward or inward before applying pressure - if they rotate, reposition before continuing

common_errors.error: Committing fully to arm attack without securing proper grip first
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes the partial submission and you lose North-South position entirely during the scramble
common_errors.correction: Establish complete wrist and elbow control before shifting any weight toward the submission finish

common_errors.error: Neglecting to control opponent's free arm during attack
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses free arm to frame, push your hips, or grab their trapped arm to prevent the break
common_errors.correction: Pin or control their opposite arm before committing to the reverse armbar finish

common_errors.error: Applying submission pressure too quickly in training
common_errors.consequence: Risk of elbow injury to training partner due to the unusual breaking angle they may not immediately recognize
common_errors.correction: Apply pressure progressively and give partner time to tap - this angle is less familiar than standard armbars

training_progressions.description: Learn arm isolation mechanics from North-South without resistance. Practice identifying exposed arms and establishing wrist and elbow control. Drill the breaking angle positioning slowly with cooperative partner.

Partner provides light North-South escape attempts while you recognize arm exposure windows. Practice entering the reverse armbar when they frame or reach. Build muscle memory for grip establishment sequence.
Chain reverse armbar with North-South choke and kimura attacks. When one attack is defended, flow to the next. Practice recognizing which attack each defensive reaction exposes.
Apply in positional sparring from North-South with full resistance. Focus on recognizing genuine opportunities versus forced attacks. Integrate into your complete North-South control game.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Position opponent's elbow directly across your hip bone for maximum leverage. Your hip acts as the fulcrum point while you control wrist with both hands. Particularly effective against larger opponents.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent's arm extends toward your lower body during escape attempt

variants_and_adaptations.description: Trap opponent's arm against your chest by pinching your elbows tight while controlling their wrist. Create breaking pressure by arching your back and expanding your chest.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When arm is caught higher near your chest during their framing attempt

variants_and_adaptations.description: If opponent begins escaping during the attack, roll with them while maintaining arm control, potentially finishing the armbar from the new position or transitioning to standard armbar mechanics.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent successfully bridges but you maintain grip on the isolated arm

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary goal of the Reverse Armbar from North-South?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary goal is to hyperextend the opponent's elbow joint by positioning their arm across your hips or chest while maintaining North-South control. Unlike traditional armbars, you maintain the north-south alignment while creating a breaking angle that attacks the arm from an unconventional direction, making it difficult for opponents to recognize and defend.

knowledge_assessment.question: What position do you start the Reverse Armbar from and why is this position advantageous?
knowledge_assessment.answer: This technique starts from North-South top position. This position is advantageous because the perpendicular body alignment creates natural arm exposure opportunities when opponents try to escape. Their arms must extend to create frames or push your body, which exposes them to isolation and attack. The heavy chest pressure also limits their defensive options.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the critical grip requirements for the Reverse Armbar?
knowledge_assessment.answer: You need to control both the wrist and elbow simultaneously. Wrist control ensures their palm faces upward or inward, preventing the arm rotation that would eliminate your breaking angle. Elbow control traps the joint against your body as the fulcrum point. Without controlling both, opponents can retract or rotate the arm to escape.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent begins rotating their arm as you apply pressure - how do you adjust?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Stop applying breaking pressure immediately and reposition. Adjust your hip position to find a new breaking angle that accounts for their arm rotation, or release the reverse armbar and transition to kimura control on the rotated arm. Forcing the submission against improper alignment risks losing position and potentially injuring the joint at an awkward angle.

knowledge_assessment.question: When is the optimal timing window to attack the Reverse Armbar?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The optimal timing is when your opponent extends an arm during escape attempts or frame creation. When they push against your chest or hips to create space, or when they reach for your legs during bridge attempts, their arm becomes exposed. Attack during their action, not after they've retracted to defensive position.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you maintain position if the submission fails and opponent begins escaping?
knowledge_assessment.answer: If the submission fails, immediately release the arm attack and reestablish heavy chest pressure in North-South. You can also transition to side control by spinning your body parallel to theirs. Never chase a failing submission at the cost of position - maintaining control allows you to attack again when a new opportunity presents.

knowledge_assessment.question: What submission attacks chain naturally with the Reverse Armbar from North-South?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The Reverse Armbar chains with the North-South choke and kimura. When opponents defend their arms by keeping elbows tight, their neck becomes exposed for the choke. When they defend their neck by framing with arms, those arms become exposed for reverse armbar or kimura. These three attacks create a triangle of threats where defending one exposes another.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent posts their hand on your hip to prevent your chest from settling - how do you capitalize?
knowledge_assessment.answer: This posted hand is exactly the arm exposure you need. Immediately secure their wrist with your near hand while trapping their elbow against your hip. Their extended arm is already in position for the reverse armbar. Apply breaking pressure by driving your hips upward while keeping their wrist controlled - they've essentially handed you the submission.

knowledge_assessment.question: What distinguishes the Reverse Armbar from a standard armbar attack?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The standard armbar requires positioning your hips beside the opponent's head with legs controlling their body. The Reverse Armbar maintains the North-South alignment while creating a breaking angle across your hips or chest. This requires less positional transition, can be attacked more quickly when arms are exposed, and comes from an angle opponents train less against.

knowledge_assessment.question: How should you apply pressure for training safety given this technique's unusual angle?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Apply pressure progressively and slowly, giving your training partner adequate time to tap. The breaking angle is less familiar than standard armbars, so partners may not immediately recognize the danger. Communicate with your partner about pressure levels and stop immediately upon tap. In competition, the same progressive application helps ensure a clean finish rather than a sloppy escape.

safety_considerations: The Reverse Armbar attacks the elbow from an unconventional angle that many practitioners are unfamiliar with. This unfamiliarity increases injury risk because training partners may not recognize the submission danger as quickly as they would a traditional armbar. Always apply pressure progressively in training and give your partner adequate time to tap. The elbow joint is vulnerable to hyperextension injuries that can cause ligament damage or dislocation. Never jerk or explosively apply the breaking pressure. If your partner's arm is positioned awkwardly or they're resisting with poor alignment, release and reposition rather than forcing the submission. Practitioners with existing elbow injuries or hypermobility should be cautious receiving this technique. When drilling, start with zero resistance and build up slowly as both partners become comfortable with the mechanics and tap timing.
position_integration: The Reverse Armbar integrates into the North-South control system as a key submission threat that complements the North-South choke and kimura attacks. When opponents defend their neck against the choke by tucking their chin and framing with their arms, those framing arms become vulnerable to the Reverse Armbar. Conversely, when they keep arms tight to defend arm attacks, their neck becomes exposed. This creates a systematic attack triangle where each defensive choice opens a different offensive opportunity. The technique also serves as a position-retention tool - even threatening the armbar forces opponents to keep arms tight, which reduces their ability to frame and escape. From a game-planning perspective, developing all three attacks from North-South transforms this position from a control checkpoint into a genuine finishing position.
